question: Four years ago the owner of a shopping center leased a store in the center for a 10-year term to a pharmacistfor use as a drugstore. Last year the owner purchased a parcel of land immediately adjacent to the shopping center. That parcel wasimproved with a building that, at the time of the owner's purchase and for ten years earlier, was occupied inpart by a food supermarket and in part by a discount drugstore, under leases which the prior owner assignedto the owner. The owner reconstructed the common facilities of both shopping centers to integrate them and combine themso that, to the public, the two centers appeared as a larger single development. The pharmacist learned that the lease of the discount drugstore was about to expire and that the ownerplanned to enter into a new lease of the same space with the discount drugstore. The pharmacist protested the proposed new lease, but the owner declared his intention to go forward with it. The pharmacist brought an appropriate action to enjoin the new lease to the discount drugstore as a violationof the covenant in the pharmacist's lease. If the court finds for the owner, what will be the likely reason?
options: The covenant does not apply to the owner's actions as he did not directly lease the space to another drugstore but bought a property which already had a lease with a drugstore.
The owner's purchase and integration of the adjacent parcel of land effectively nullifies the existing covenant.
The drugstore use on the adjacent parcel was in existence when the owner and the pharmacist firstentered into the lease.
The discount drugstore on the adjacent parcel is not considered a 'new' lease, but a continuation of an existing one.
A covenant cannot restrict the use of land not owned by the covenantor when the covenant wascreated.
The owner has the right to lease any part of his property to any business, regardless of existing leases.
The pharmacist did not adequately express his concerns to the owner before initiating legal action.
A covenant that attempts to restrict competition is invalid as against public policy even if it runs with theland.
The covenant in the pharmacist's lease can be fairly construed as to apply only to the original shoppingcenter premises.
The covenant is not applicable as the shopping centers were considered separate entities at the time of the lease agreement.
gold: The covenant in the pharmacist's lease can be fairly construed as to apply only to the original shoppingcenter premises.

Yes, because the homeowner did not physically enter the neighbor's property.

The defendant argued at trial that he only intended to scare the victim to shut him up, and that he did not have the intent to kill. Is the defendant guilty of murder?
options: Yes, his use of a deadly weapon demonstrated the requisite intent to kill.
No, his behavior was reckless but not intentional.
No, the defendant was just trying to scare the victim, not kill him.
No, defendant was trying to protect himself from the victim's aggressive behavior.
No, defendant was in a heated argument and his judgement was clouded, so he didn't have the intent to kill.
Yes, as he should have known that using a deadly weapon could result in death, showing implied intent.
No, defendant responded to the victim's provocation and did not intend to kill.
Yes, his use of a deadly weapon shows he had the intent to cause grievous harm, which resulted in death.
No, he acted on the spur of the moment and could not have formed the requisite intent.
Yes, because he intended to scare the victim with a deadly weapon, which is enough for a murder charge.
gold: Yes, his use of a deadly weapon demonstrated the requisite intent to kill.
